title: Monitor the quality assurance in Rooibos processing

lessons.title: What quality means for rooibos
lessons.html:
Good tea is safe, clean and the right colour

Quality assurance (QA) means checking every step of the work so that the final tea is good every time. It is better to stop problems early than to find bad tea at the end.

What buyers check

Quality pointWhat good looks like
ColourEven red-brown for fermented tea; green for green rooibos
Smell and tasteSweet, pleasant, no sour, mouldy or smoky smell
Cut sizeShort, even pieces as the buyer asks
DrynessDry enough to store without mould
CleanlinessNo stones, sand, weeds, plastic, string, hair, insects
Food safetyNo harmful germs or chemicals

Why it matters

The processor and buyer test samples from every batch. If tea fails, it can be sold at a low price or rejected. Bad quality can also make people sick and damage the name of South African rooibos.

Your job in QA

  • Know what good tea looks and smells like.
  • Check the tea at each step.
  • Write down what you check.
  • Tell the supervisor at once when something is wrong.
  • Keep bad tea apart so it does not get mixed with good tea.

Know what good looks like

Ask your supervisor to show you a sample of good tea and a sample with problems. Look at the colour, smell it, and feel how dry it is. When you know what good tea is like, it is much easier to notice when something is wrong.

lessons.title: Checks at each processing step
lessons.html:
Check, write down, report

When the harvest arrives

  • Is it rooibos only? Remove weeds and rubbish.
  • Is it fresh and not heated in the heap?
  • Write down the land and time it arrived.

Cutting

  • Are the pieces the right length?
  • Is there foreign material in the cut tea?

Bruising and fermenting

  • Was clean water used?
  • Is colour developing evenly?
  • Is the smell sweet, not sour?
  • Write down start and end times of fermenting.

Drying

  • Is the tea spread thinly and evenly?
  • Is it protected from rain, dust and animals?
  • Is it dry before bagging? The supervisor checks this.

Bagging and storage

  • Are bags clean and approved?
  • Is every bag labelled with batch and date?
  • Is the store dry, clean and free of rats and insects?
  • Are bags stacked off the floor, away from walls?

Samples

Your supervisor may ask you to take samples. Take them from different parts of the batch, put them in a clean container and label them with batch number and date. Never take samples with dirty hands.

Using a check sheet

Most farms give the team a check sheet for each batch. It has a line for each step: harvest received, cutting, bruising, fermenting, drying, bagging and storage. At each step you tick what you checked, write the time and sign your name. If something was not right, write what you saw and what was done about it. The supervisor checks and signs the sheet at the end of the day. A full, honest check sheet shows the buyer that the tea was made with care, and it helps the farm find the cause if a sample fails at the processor.

lessons.title: Dealing with problems and keeping records
lessons.html:
When tea is not right

  1. Stop – do not carry on with the bad tea.
  2. Separate – keep the problem tea apart and mark it.
  3. Report – tell the supervisor what you saw.
  4. Record – write down the batch, problem and what was done.

Never hide bad tea by mixing it with good tea. It will be found in testing and the whole batch can be rejected.

Common problems and causes

ProblemCommon cause
Green pieces in red teaUneven bruising or short fermenting
Mould or musty smellTea too wet, thick drying layers, damp store
Sand and stonesDirty harvest or dirty tea court
GermsAnimals on the court, dirty water, poor hand washing

Records

Records show that the farm did its work correctly. They help find where a problem started. Write clearly, sign and date every record. Never change a record later without the supervisor.

Learning from problems

When a problem happens, the supervisor and team should talk about why it happened and how to stop it next time. For example, if sand is often found in the tea, the team may need to sweep the court more often or fix a broken wall where wind blows sand in.

Key points

  • Quality assurance means checking every step, not only the end.
  • Good tea has the right colour, sweet smell, even cut and is clean and dry.
  • If something is wrong: stop, separate, report and record.
  • Never mix bad tea with good tea.
  • Write clear, signed and dated records.
